tier_reason: Independent third-party measurement: the z-fasta author benchmarked noodles and samtools with a public harness (bench/index/run.sh, tools/install.sh, tools/noodles_wrapper/src/main.rs), and the README names the CPU (Ryzen 9 3950X) for the same 2026-10-10 v0.3.5 run with identical numbers. It falls short of A because neither the rustc nor the C compiler version is stated anywhere, and the flags are only implied by build defaults (Rust release profile, HTSlib/samtools Makefile -O2).

corrections.claimed_speedup: bench/index/REPORT.md Table 3 (zebrac mean, warm cache): Genome 1.3640 s (noodles) vs 8.1614 s (samtools), about 6.0x faster (derived from page data); Table 4 throughput 2203.5 MiB/s vs 368.3 MiB/s. Transcriptome 0.4111 s vs 1.7112 s, about 4.2x (derived from page data). Proteome 0.0176 s vs 0.0650 s, about 3.7x (derived from page data). Synthetic scaling (Table 12, 100 records): 1000 MiB 0.3981 s vs 2.7896 s, about 7.0x (derived from page data). Peak RSS on the genome is 3.59 MiB vs 9.31 MiB.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: noodles wrapper (tools/noodles_wrapper, noodles-fasta 0.66.0, noodles-core 0.20): cargo build --locked --release with the default release profile (opt-level 3, no LTO, no custom RUSTFLAGS), rustc version not stated; binary stripped with strip --strip-unneeded. samtools 1.24 and HTSlib 1.24 built from release tarballs by tools/install.sh with plain ./configure and make and no explicit CFLAGS, so the upstream Makefile default CFLAGS = -g -Wall -O2 applies (htslib and samtools Makefiles at tag 1.24); C compiler and version not stated; samtools linked against the shared libhts; binary stripped.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, Linux x86_64, warm page cache (named in the z-fasta README for the v0.3.5 run of 2026-10-10, whose index table matches REPORT.md exactly; REPORT.md itself names no CPU).
corrections.caveats: The evidence lives in a competitor's repo: eneskemalergin/z-fasta is a Zig FASTA tool whose benchmark ranks itself first (0.3824 s on the genome, 3.6x faster than noodles); the noodles row is incidental but independent of both noodles and samtools. The noodles lane is a 373-line wrapper CLI whose index subcommand just calls noodles_fasta::fs::index and fai::fs::write; both lanes are timed as 'rm -f <fasta>.fai; <tool> index <fasta>' in bench/index/run.sh, so the comparison is symmetric. samtools is HTSlib's default -O2 build, not -O3 (same_opt_level false), though this is the shipping upstream configuration and not a crippled build. The speedup is an implementation difference, not a language effect: HTSlib 1.24 faidx.c fai_build_core walks the file one byte at a time through an inlined bgzf_getc with a per-character state machine, while noodles-fasta's io::Indexer scans BufReader chunks with memchr for line feeds and counts bases per line. Output byte-equality of the noodles .fai against samtools is not checked in the report (FAI parity covers z-fasta only; Table 2 records exit codes, not output validation). Single machine, 5 samples after warmups, warm cache only. Peak RSS is lower for noodles (3.59 MiB vs 9.31 MiB on the genome, 46.65 vs 65.49 MiB on the transcriptome); the earlier caveat calling it equal was wrong. On the smallest synthetic file (1 MiB) noodles takes 0.0037 s vs 0.0175 s for samtools, so the lead holds across sizes.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 727 stars; noodles-fasta crate 484,738 downloads on crates.io (latest 0.67.0)
corrections.why_faster: Implementation, not language: noodles-fasta's Indexer finds line ends with memchr over buffered chunks (fill_buf/consume) and counts bases per line, while HTSlib 1.24 fai_build_core processes every byte through bgzf_getc and a per-character branchy state machine; the Rust build is also opt-level 3 against HTSlib's default -O2.

notes: Numbers match REPORT.md Tables 3-4 and the README; the harness, install script and wrapper are public and the timed commands are symmetric. Downgraded A to B because no compiler versions are stated and samtools is the default -O2 build; the win is memchr-based line scanning against HTSlib's byte-at-a-time loop, and noodles' .fai output was not checked against samtools. HTSlib (samtools' library) is already listed in wave 8.

tier_reason: The peer-reviewed comparison with Kraken2 was seen only through search-result snippets (PMC, Nature and bioRxiv unreachable: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so under the snippet-only rule it cannot hold B. The paper's artifact repo (bluenote-1577/sylph-test/times) carries first-party /usr/bin/time outputs for Kraken2 and sylph, but with no CPU model, no Kraken2 command or database, and no statement of which files back the paper figure.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper abstract (search-snippet text only, PMC and bioRxiv blocked): for multisample profiling sylph took more than 10-fold less CPU time than Kraken2 and used 30-fold less memory. Artifact repo bluenote-1577/sylph-test/times: kraken2.time reports 72,628.96 s user + 5,582.99 s system, 1:47:10 wall, 73,857,640 kB max RSS; sylph_sketch_reads.time (sylph sketch -t 20 on 45 paired read sets) 2,186.65 s + 101.51 s, 5:48 wall, 2,831,688 kB; sylph_contain_gtdb.time (sylph contain -t 20, 45 samples) 1,497.39 s + 57.60 s, 2:00 wall, 9,567,920 kB. If these files are the paired runs, sylph uses about 20x less CPU time, about 13.7x less wall time and about 7.7x less peak memory (derived from page data; pairing not confirmed, and the 7.7x memory ratio does not match the paper's 30-fold). README: 'can be > 50x faster than other methods' (no baseline named).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust; Cargo release profile sets panic=abort and lto=true. The sylph version, toolchain and Kraken2 build used for the paper timings are not stated in the artifact repo files I saw.
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: the PMC, Nature and bioRxiv pages are unreachable from this environment, so the paper's Kraken2 figures come from search-result text; paper tables, thread counts, CPU model, database sizes and the MetaPhlAn comparison were not seen. The two tools differ in algorithm (sylph sketches reads and genomes with subsampled k-mers and estimates containment-based abundance; Kraken2 classifies every read's k-mers against a large hash table), so the ratios compare tools with different outputs and are not a language effect. The sylph-test/times files are raw /usr/bin/time outputs with no CPU model: Kraken2 ran a ./scripts/kraken2.sh that is not in the repo (404), at about 12 cores of CPU (1216%), while sylph ran with -t 20; the files do not say which database Kraken2 used or that they are the pair behind the paper figure, and their memory ratio (about 7.7x) differs from the paper's 30-fold. The README names no baseline for its '>50x faster' claim and compares precision with 'Kraken', not speed. The repo LICENSE file is MIT only, although Cargo.toml declares 'MIT OR Apache-2.0' and no Apache-2.0 text ships. Kraken2 is not in the catalog's verified lists. Documentation moved to sylph-docs.github.io, which is blocked here.

notes: Downgraded B to C: the peer-reviewed Kraken2 comparison is snippet-only, and the artifact repo's raw time files (Kraken2 78,212 CPU-seconds against sylph's 3,843 for sketch plus contain, about 20x derived) are first-party, lack a CPU model and Kraken2 command, and give a 7.7x memory ratio rather than the paper's 30x. Sketch containment against read classification is an algorithmic win, not a Rust-over-C++ one. License corrected to MIT (LICENSE file); baseline_in_list left as recorded, though Kraken2 has no catalog entry.
